title: Securing the quantum stack: export controls, choke points and strategic competition
author: IISS
text:
AuthorsDongyoun Cho Senior Fellow for Advanced Technologies, National Security and DefenceAbout Dongyoun ChoDr Maria Shagina @maria_shaginaSenior Fellow for Geo-economics and StrategyAbout Dr Maria Shagina

Online Analysis29th July 2026

Securing the quantum stack: export controls, choke points and strategic competitionThe US and its allies have built aligned export controls on quantum technology, targeting supply-chain choke points before the industry matures. Their success will depend not only on denying rivals access, but also on sustaining the allied ecosystem.  

Since 2024, the United States and several allies have rapidly converged on quantum-computing export controls. Driven by national-security concerns, these measures have been coordinated through plurilateral arrangements rather than traditional multilateral export-control regimes. The deadlock within the Wassenaar Arrangement (WA) – an export-control regime that governs conventional weapons and dual-use technologies – following Russia’s obstruction of updates to its control lists since 2022, has pushed like-minded countries to develop largely aligned national controls outside the formal multilateral framework. The result is a patchwork of broadly harmonised, but legally distinct, export-control regimes.
Quantum computing illustrates how export controls on emerging technologies face fundamentally different challenges than those applied to mature industries. The central challenge is balancing two competing objectives: preventing military exploitation by strategic rivals while also avoiding restrictions that would unnecessarily impede scientific research, commercialisation and innovation. Rather than starting with a single stage of production, the controls are applied almost across the entire quantum ‘stack’ from initiation – from complete quantum computers, enabling components and equipment to advanced materials. Unlike export controls on mature technologies, which typically begin downstream in the supply chains and tighten as they move upstream, quantum controls seek to shape the development of the ecosystem at an early stage while preserving room for legitimate research collaboration. In effect, on quantum, governments are moving from reactive regulation to anticipatory containment, seeking to constrain future military capabilities before they become commercially widespread.
The quantum stack and its choke points
Quantum computing presents unusually difficult challenges for export controls because its ecosystem is inherently international: no single country dominates the supply chain, whether specialised materials, cryogenic equipment, hardware, software, fabrication or algorithms. But dominant nodes do exist. The effectiveness of any export-control regime will therefore depend less on the comprehensiveness of its control lists than on whether it captures the small number of geographically dispersed firms and facilities – critical nodes – whose technologies are indispensable, difficult to substitute and located within jurisdictions willing to coordinate restrictions. By applying controls across the entire quantum supply chain, Western governments seek to deny adversaries access to these critical nodes while reducing the need for continual regulatory adjustments to close emerging loopholes.
Where these nodes sit becomes visible only when the supply chain is disaggregated into its three layers: materials, equipment and components. At the materials layer, isotopically enriched silicon-28, required for high-performance spin qubits, is only available in commercially meaningful volumes from a few facilities worldwide; helium-3, indispensable to dilution refrigeration, is a scarce by-product of tritium decay concentrated in US and Russian stockpiles; and electronic-grade synthetic diamond, the substrate for many quantum-sensing and quantum-memory devices, is dominated in the West by Element Six, a subsidiary of De Beers based in the United Kingdom – described as the ‘only proven Western supplier’ of quantum-grade material. At the equipment layer, superconducting quantum computers – the architecture at the centre of the US controls, as shown in Table 1 – cannot run without dilution refrigerators, produced at scale by only a handful of suppliers led by Bluefors in Finland and Oxford Instruments in the UK. At the component layer, the control electronics and cryogenic assemblies that connect qubits to conventional (‘classical’) electronics remain concentrated in a small number of European, Japanese and US firms. Europe fields fewer frontier quantum-computing firms than the US, yet it holds disproportionate leverage across the enabling layers (see Table 1).  

National measures
The US has established the most comprehensive regime among Western jurisdictions. In September 2024, the Bureau of Industry and Security adopted an Interim Final Rule introducing controls on advanced quantum computers exceeding specified technical-performance thresholds, quantum electronic assemblies and components, cryogenic systems and probing equipment, selected silicon- and germanium-based materials, software for development and production, and associated technology and technical data. The controls primarily focus on gate-based quantum-computing architectures, with control thresholds defined by qubit counts and error rates – in effect, how large and how reliable a machine is – while simultaneously introducing worldwide licensing requirements and outbound-investment restrictions targeting China’s quantum sector.
Recognising that quantum innovation depends on international collaboration, the US also incorporated notable safeguards. The Interim Final Rule introduced licence exceptions for countries implementing equivalent controls – including Australia, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway and the UK – and replaced traditional deemed-export restrictions for foreign nationals working within the US with record-keeping requirements. This represents a marked departure from conventional American export-control practice, reflecting policymakers’ concern that overly restrictive controls could undermine the research ecosystem on which US technological leadership ultimately depends.
Under US President Donald Trump’s second administration, policy has increasingly focused on combining export controls with supply-chain resilience and allied technology coordination. In June 2026, the administration issued Executive Order 14413, ‘Ushering in the Next Frontier of Quantum Innovation’, with the objective of preventing adversaries from acquiring quantum-enabling technologies and harmonising export-control policies with those of international allies and partners. By participating in initiatives such as the Quantum Development Group, a forum of 13 like-minded countries, Washington seeks to promote resilient and reliable supply chains, deepen research collaboration and strengthen investment security.
Within the European Union, institutional constraints initially complicated the adoption of comparable controls. Because the EU Dual-use Regulation 2021/821 is closely linked to multilateral export-control regimes, the WA deadlock prevented Brussels from introducing autonomous EU-wide restrictions. Instead, six member states – Finland, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain – used Article 9 of the Dual-use Regulation to introduce national controls largely mirroring the United States’ approach. Although this preserved alignment with Washington, it also created regulatory fragmentation within the single market. In September 2025, the European Commission introduced autonomous EU-level controls applicable across all member states to address this problem. The new ‘500-series’ of EU-only entries, in force since November 2025, covers a range of emerging dual-use technologies, including quantum computing. The new controls largely replace the national controls previously adopted by member states, although some limited national measures remain in place.
Other allies followed a similar path. The UK introduced national export controls on quantum and other emerging technologies in 2024; Japan followed in July of that year with a set of controls focused primarily on quantum computers, cryogenic circuits and related enabling technologies. In December 2025, the UK mirrored changes in the EU’s list and replaced national entries (PL9013–9015) with ‘500-series’ controls.
Where the controls bind – and where they leak
As demonstrated in Table 1, the measures described above regulate unevenly – and this unevenness follows the layers. At the equipment and component layers, lists and choke points largely align: restrictions on cryogenic systems and quantum electronic assemblies are enforceable because production is concentrated in a few allied jurisdictions, and licensing decisions taken in Helsinki, London or Washington can materially shape what a rival programme can assemble. Yet even within a choke point, misalignment may lead to leaks: in 2022, after the UK refused an export licence for Oxford Instruments equipment, the Beijing Academy of Quantum Information Sciences purchased three dilution refrigerators from Bluefors – at a time when Finland’s own control list had yet to be finalised. Here, the EU’s harmonised controls matter more than their modest framing suggests: several of the most consequential nodes in the global quantum supply chain are European, and the credibility of any plurilateral denial strategy depends on whether Brussels tackles the uneven regulatory playing field effectively. At the materials layer, by contrast, coverage is partial. Enriched silicon- and germanium-based materials appear on the US lists, but helium-3 and quantum-grade diamond fall largely outside the quantum-specific controls, governed instead by older and unevenly applied provisions. Moreover, listing an item in itself does not confer leverage: part of the world’s limited silicon-28 capability sits in Russia and China, making a listed material as much a dependency as a lever.
The controls falter where the underlying node is contestable and, increasingly, where the layer in question is left exposed. Export restrictions do not merely deny; they signal. Each controlled item advertises a dependency worth eliminating, and China has responded accordingly. Within two years of the first Western listings, Chinese entities QuantumCTek and Anhui Quantum Computing Engineering Research Centre had begun factory production of a domestic dilution refrigerator. In diamond substrates, Chinese suppliers such as Chenguang Machinery & Electric Equipment have moved to court academic customers lacking certainty due to Western restrictions. Where the production base is broader – control electronics, lasers, much of the photonics layer – restrictions raise costs and buy time, but supply chains reconfigure through alternative jurisdictions faster than lists can be updated. Controls on such nodes function as friction, not denial: they slow acquisition without preventing it. Dependence, moreover, runs both ways: Beijing restricts exports of sub-6-kelvin cryogenic technology and quantum encryption, even as China’s own programmes rely on US and Russian helium-3 stockpiles.
From anticipation to absorption
Export controls alone cannot secure long-term technological leadership. Quantum development also depends on resilient supply chains for critical minerals, many of which remain heavily concentrated in China, as well as complementary policies on investment screening and industrial strategy. Without investment screening, strategically important firms remain vulnerable to foreign acquisitions; without industrial policy, many promising quantum companies struggle to commercialise technologies and to scale production.
Recognising this broader challenge, governments have increasingly complemented export controls with industrial policy. In 2018 the US enacted the National Quantum Initiative Act, while in May 2026 the administration signed letters of intent to invest US$2 billion in nine quantum companies, taking minority equity stakes in each. Two-thirds of this investment was directed to two dedicated quantum-chip foundries (IBM’s new Anderon and GlobalFoundries) to build domestic-manufacturing capacity for quantum-grade wafers. The UK committed £2.5bn for to its 2024–34 National Quantum Strategy, including a dedicated public-procurement programme; the EU continues to invest through the €1bn Quantum Technologies Flagship programme; and Japan designated 2025 its ‘first year of quantum industrialisation’. Together, export controls, investment screening and industrial policy form an integrated toolkit for shaping the early quantum market.
But the toolkit’s logic points beyond anticipatory containment. Export controls can slow down a rival’s accumulation of capability, but they cannot, by themselves, sustain the ecosystem on which the controlling side’s own advantage rests. Choke-point leverage is an asset with maintenance costs: a dilution-refrigerator maker or an isotope-enrichment facility remains a strategic asset only for as long as it remains a viable company. If controls shrink these firms’ markets, or if buyers hedge away from suppliers entangled in licensing uncertainty, the once-critical node erodes – and the leverage erodes with it. Denial therefore has to be matched by absorption: the capacity of allied markets to sustain investment, demand and industrial capability in precisely the nodes their control lists now highlight. As quantum technologies move out of the laboratory and towards deployment, the decisive question is no longer which technologies to deny an adversary, but which nodes of one’s own ecosystem to sustain.
